# Telapattajātaka (Ja 96)

**Section:** Jātaka (ja)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Telapattajātaka* (Ja 96), rendered in English as *The Pot of Oil*, is a story in the Pali Jātaka collection [SuttaCentral]. In the Dhammapada commentary, the narrative is also identified under the alternative title *Takkasilā Jātaka* [Burlingame 1921]. According to its commentarial opening, the Buddha recounted the jātaka while dwelling in a forest near the town of Desaka in the Sumbha country, prompted by the *Janapadakalyāṇī Sutta* [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877].

The introductory setting and simile concern a man tasked with carrying a vessel brimful of oil (*telapatta*) along a road flanked by a crowd gazing upon the most beautiful woman of the country (*janapadakalyāṇī*), closely followed by a guard with a drawn sword instructed to decapitate him if a single drop spills [Lang 2003; Fausböll 1877]. This serves as an illustration of the rigorous self-restraint and vigilance needed for cultivating mindfulness directed to the body (*kāyagatāsati*) [Fausböll 1877]. In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta is a prince traveling from Benares to Takkasilā across a wilderness infested by lustful, flesh-eating demonesses (*yakkhinī*s) [Sutherland 1991; Appleton 2010]. While his five companions succumb one by one to sensory temptations and are eaten, the prince exercises resolute self-control and resists their charms [Appleton 2006; Appleton 2010]. One *yakkhinī* follows him disguised as his wife; after failing to entice the prince, she seduces the king of Takkasilā, causing the royal household to be slaughtered before the Bodhisatta expels the demons and is installed upon the royal throne [Burlingame 1921; Appleton 2010]. The prose also contains an early textual description of protective ritual (*paritta*), wherein the prince arms himself with protective sand and thread bestowed by *paccekabuddha*s [Gombrich 1991; Appleton 2010].

Neither SuttaCentral nor DharmaNexus reports any internal canonical Pali reuse or close cross-language parallels for the verse text [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. However, comparative narrative studies indicate that the plot of the *Telapattajātaka* is combined with the *Valāhassa-jātaka* in northern Buddhist collections such as the *Divyāvadāna* and the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* [Appleton 2010]. In addition, five verses belonging to the Citta-group of the Dhammapada are cited in the extant Jātaka commentary on this story [Barua 1921].
